questions.q: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (BSA), replacing the Indian Evidence Act 1872, came into force on:
o: 26 January 2024
1 July 2024
15 August 2023
25 December 2023
questions.src: The BSA came into force on 1 July 2024, alongside the BNS and BNSS, though it received Presidential assent in December 2023.

questions.q: Under Section 4 BSA, evidence may generally be given only of:
o: Any fact whatsoever, with no restriction
Facts in issue AND relevant facts, and no others
Only facts personally witnessed by a judge
Only documents, never oral testimony
questions.src: Section 4 establishes the foundational admissibility gate — evidence is confined to facts in issue and relevant facts.

questions.q: "Facts in Issue," as distinguished from "Relevant Facts," refer to:
o: Facts entirely unconnected to the dispute
Facts from which the existence/non-existence of the right or liability asserted or denied necessarily follows
Only facts admitted by both parties
Only facts proven by documentary evidence
questions.src: Facts in Issue directly determine the outcome of the claimed right/liability, distinct from Relevant Facts which merely help prove or disprove them.

questions.q: Under the BSA, electronic records are classified as:
o: Always inadmissible in any proceeding
PRIMARY evidence — a change from the IEA's treatment of them as secondary evidence
Only admissible in criminal cases, never civil
The same as oral testimony, with no special rules
questions.src: The BSA reclassifies electronic records as primary evidence, reflecting the significance of digital records in modern litigation.

questions.q: Under Section 25 BSA, an admission is:
o: Automatically conclusive proof of the matter admitted
NOT conclusive proof, but may operate as an estoppel preventing the person from later denying it
Entirely irrelevant to any proceeding
Only relevant in criminal cases
questions.src: Admissions carry evidentiary weight but are not automatically conclusive — their real force often comes through the doctrine of estoppel.

questions.q: A confession made by an accused person TO A POLICE OFFICER is generally:
o: Fully admissible against the accused without restriction
NOT admissible against the accused, reflecting concerns about reliability of custodial confessions
Admissible only if written in the accused's own hand
Admissible only in civil proceedings
questions.src: Confessions to police officers are generally excluded, a longstanding protection against potentially coerced or unreliable custodial confessions.

questions.q: Under the narrow exception in Section 23 BSA, where a fact is discovered as a consequence of information from an accused in police custody:
o: The entire confession becomes admissible without limit
So much of the information as DISTINCTLY relates to the fact discovered may be proved
Nothing from that information can ever be used
Only the police officer's opinion about the confession is admissible
questions.src: This narrow exception allows only the verifiable, discovery-linked portion of an otherwise inadmissible confession into evidence.

questions.q: Under Section 26(a) BSA, a dying declaration is relevant:
o: Only in criminal cases of murder specifically
In ANY proceeding, civil or criminal, in which the cause of that person's death comes into question
Only if the declarant expected to die at the time of making the statement
Only if recorded by a judge personally
questions.src: Indian law takes a broader approach than English law — the declaration is relevant in both civil and criminal proceedings, without requiring the declarant to have expected death.

questions.q: In Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay (1958), the Supreme Court held that a dying declaration:
o: Can never be the sole basis of a conviction under any circumstances
Requires NO absolute corroboration as a rule of law — a true, voluntary declaration can alone sustain a conviction
Is only relevant if the declarant was a public official
Must always be corroborated by at least two independent witnesses
questions.src: Khushal Rao established that a dying declaration is substantive evidence in its own right, not requiring mandatory corroboration if found true and voluntary.

questions.q: In Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002), the Supreme Court clarified that medical certification of the declarant's fitness of mind:
o: Is an absolute, mandatory legal precondition for any valid dying declaration
Is preferred and strengthens reliability, but is NOT a strict legal precondition ("sine qua non") for admissibility
Makes the dying declaration automatically inadmissible if absent
Is irrelevant to the dying declaration's evidentiary value
questions.src: Laxman confirmed medical certification is a preferred but not mandatory element — the real test is whether the declarant was actually in a fit state of mind.

questions.q: The general rule for Burden of Proof states that:
o: The Court itself must always independently investigate and prove all facts
Whoever desires the Court to give judgment based on facts they assert must prove those facts exist
The burden always lies on the defendant regardless of the claim
No party ever bears any burden of proof
questions.src: This is the foundational "he who asserts must prove" principle underlying the burden of proof framework.

questions.q: The standard of proof in a CRIMINAL case, as distinguished from a civil case, is:
o: Preponderance of probabilities, identical to civil cases
Proof BEYOND REASONABLE DOUBT — a materially higher standard than the civil standard
No standard of proof is required in criminal cases
Only the accused's own confession is required
questions.src: Criminal cases require the higher "beyond reasonable doubt" standard, reflecting the severe consequences of wrongful conviction, versus civil cases' preponderance-of-probabilities standard.

questions.q: Under the BSA's presumption framework, "Shall Presume" means the Court:
o: Has complete discretion whether to presume the fact or not
MUST regard the fact as proved, unless and until it is disproved — a mandatory but rebuttable presumption
Can never presume that fact under any circumstances
Must treat the fact as an irrebuttable, conclusive matter
questions.src: "Shall Presume" is mandatory but still rebuttable — distinct from the discretionary "May Presume" and the irrebuttable "Conclusive Proof."

questions.q: "Conclusive Proof," as a term used in the BSA, means that once one fact is proved:
o: The Court has full discretion on whether to accept the other fact
The Court SHALL regard the other fact as proved, and NO evidence to disprove it is permitted — an irrebuttable presumption
Both facts must be independently proved separately
The presumption can always be freely disproved by either party
questions.src: Conclusive Proof is the strongest form of presumption — genuinely irrebuttable, unlike the other two presumption categories.

questions.q: The Doctrine of Estoppel under the BSA prevents a person from:
o: Ever testifying in any future proceeding
Later denying the truth of something they intentionally caused another person to believe and act upon
Being sued for any civil wrong whatsoever
Filing any future legal claim of any kind
questions.src: Estoppel operates as a rule of evidence preventing inconsistent assertions where another party relied on an earlier representation.

questions.q: A witness is generally considered COMPETENT to testify UNLESS the Court finds they are prevented from understanding questions or giving rational answers due to:
o: Simply being under 18 years of age
Tender years, extreme old age, disease of body or mind, or similar cause
Being a family member of a party
Having a different religion than the parties
questions.src: Competency is based on genuine capacity to understand and respond rationally, not an automatic bar based on age or relationship alone.

questions.q: A "Hostile Witness" is a witness who:
o: Refuses to appear in court at all
Testifies against the interest of the party who called them, or resiles from an earlier statement
Is always disqualified from testifying further
Can never be cross-examined by anyone
questions.src: A hostile witness unexpectedly turns against the calling party's case, permitting that party (with Court permission) to cross-examine their own witness.

questions.q: The correct order of witness examination is:
o: Cross-Examination, then Examination-in-Chief, then Re-Examination
Examination-in-Chief, then Cross-Examination, then Re-Examination
Re-Examination, then Cross-Examination, then Examination-in-Chief
There is no fixed order at all
questions.src: This is the standard, settled sequence: the calling party questions first, the opposing party cross-examines, then limited re-examination follows.

questions.q: "Leading Questions" (questions suggesting the desired answer) are generally:
o: Permitted freely in both examination-in-chief and cross-examination
PROHIBITED in examination-in-chief, but generally PERMITTED in cross-examination
Prohibited in all forms of witness examination without exception
Only permitted in re-examination
questions.src: This asymmetric rule reflects the different purposes — chief examination should elicit the witness's own account, while cross-examination legitimately tests it through suggestive questioning.

questions.q: Under Section 128 BSA (spousal privilege), communications made between spouses DURING the marriage:
o: Can always be freely disclosed by either spouse without restriction
Are generally privileged — neither spouse can be compelled to disclose them, even after the marriage ends (subject to exceptions)
Lose all privilege the moment the marriage ends
Are never protected under any circumstances
questions.src: This privilege protects marital communications from compelled disclosure, generally surviving even after the marriage itself ends.

questions.q: "Primary Evidence" of a document refers to:
o: Any certified copy of a document
The ORIGINAL document itself, produced for the Court's inspection
Only oral testimony about a document's contents
A summary prepared by a lawyer
questions.src: Primary evidence is the original document itself — regarded as the strongest, most direct form of documentary proof.

questions.q: Under the BSA, a document from proper custody that is 30 YEARS OLD or more generally benefits from:
o: No special treatment whatsoever
A presumption of genuineness, shifting the burden to the party challenging its authenticity
Automatic exclusion from evidence regardless of content
Treatment as oral evidence rather than documentary evidence
questions.src: This presumption eases the burden of formally proving very old documents, provided they come from proper custody and show no suspicion of tampering.

questions.q: In Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014), the Supreme Court held that secondary electronic evidence (like a print-out) is admissible:
o: Automatically, with no further requirements
ONLY if accompanied by a certificate satisfying the statutory requirements for authenticating electronic records
Never, under any circumstances
Only if approved in advance by the police
questions.src: This case established the mandatory certification requirement for secondary electronic evidence, remaining highly relevant under the BSA framework.

questions.q: "Exclusion of Oral Evidence by Documentary Evidence" (Chapter VI, BSA) generally means that once contract terms are reduced to writing:
o: Oral evidence of those terms becomes freely admissible alongside the document
No evidence of those terms may generally be given except the document itself (or admissible secondary evidence), subject to specified exceptions
The written document becomes entirely irrelevant
Only the opposing party can rely on the written document
questions.src: This rule generally excludes oral evidence contradicting/varying a written contract's terms, subject to exceptions like proving fraud or mistake.

questions.q: An "Accomplice" who testifies against an accused is:
o: Never competent to testify under any circumstances
Competent to testify, though courts generally look for corroboration as a matter of prudence, not an absolute legal bar
Automatically believed without question by the Court
Only permitted to testify in civil cases
questions.src: Accomplice evidence is admissible but treated with judicial caution — corroboration is generally sought as a matter of prudent practice, though not a strict legal requirement barring conviction otherwise.
